title: Pick the wall
brief: A chunk is about to be returned. Who decides whether this caller may see it: the index, your code, the source system or the shape of your infrastructure? Access selectivity, rule richness, revocation speed and where the content lives are all still open.

blocks.text: Six places to enforce the wall

blocks.md:
Ask one question of every option: **which stages see denied text?** A post-filter lets it reach your code, rerankers, logs and caches. A pre-filter keeps it inside the index. A live check asks the source of truth. Delegation never copies the content. A physical wall removes the need for a per-document filter between tenants.

Most real systems combine two: a pre-filter for the bulk of traffic and a live check on the top hits of restricted tiers. That combination is design reasoning from the options below, not a vendor pattern. The model is never one of the options [[r22]].

blocks.title: ACL enforcement options
blocks.intro: Each option names where it wins, where it loses and what flips the choice.

options.name: Post-filter in your code
options.summary: Retrieve the top k, then drop what the caller cannot see.
pros: Code can express any rule, including deny and sharing links
cons: Wastes top k when access is selective, so you over-fetch
Denied text reaches rerankers, logs and caches first
options.bestWhen: Almost every document is visible to almost every caller and the rules are too rich to precompute.
options.avoidWhen: Callers see a small slice of a large corpus, or denied text must never leave the index.

options.name: Pre-filter in the index
options.summary: Put the permission predicate inside the query: a security filter field (GA) or native ACL fields (preview).
pros: Top k stays full of visible documents
Denied text stays in the index
cons: The ACL copy lags the source
Allow-lists only, so deny entries must be flattened
Filtered ANN recall can drop at high selectivity
options.bestWhen: Permissions are group based, some sync lag is tolerable and the content is already copied into the index.
options.avoidWhen: Revocation must take effect in seconds, or deny rules and links cannot be flattened.

options.name: Pre-filter plus live check on top hits
options.summary: Filter in the index, then ask the source of truth about the few hits that survive.
pros: Closes the sync-lag window for the hits that matter
The source evaluates deny rules and links exactly
cons: Adds latency and load on the source for every query
Needs a source API that answers per document and fails closed
options.bestWhen: Restricted tiers, revocation in seconds, or rules richer than an index field can hold.
options.avoidWhen: Broad internal content where hours of lag are acceptable.

meta.v: one parallel call per checked hit

options.name: Delegate retrieval to the source
options.summary: Let the system of record retrieve with the caller's token and do not copy the content. Examples: the Microsoft 365 Copilot Retrieval API, or a remote SharePoint knowledge source in Azure AI Search.
pros: Permissions honoured at query time with nothing to sync
No copy to leak or purge
cons: Little control over ranking, chunking or filters
Retrieval API: 200 requests per user per hour, 25 results, unordered, license or pay-as-you-go (preview) needed
options.bestWhen: The content already lives in Microsoft 365 and revocation must be near immediate.
options.avoidWhen: You need custom ranking, many sources or high per-user query rates.

options.name: Index or service per tenant
options.summary: A physical wall: one index per tenant, or a separate service for the largest tenants.
pros: Per-tenant delete, export and embedding model
cons: Index caps per tier (Basic 15, S1 50, S2 and S3 200)
Cost and operations grow with tenants
Does nothing for group access inside a tenant
options.bestWhen: Few large or regulated tenants whose access is only the tenant id.
options.avoidWhen: Thousands of small tenants, or per-document ACLs inside each tenant.

options.name: Index per user
options.summary: Every user gets a private slice of the index.
cons: Copies every shared document per reader
Hits index caps after a few principals
options.bestWhen: Very few principals and highly personal data, such as a personal notes assistant.

blocks.title: Where should the wall stand?
blocks.prompt: Set how selective access is, how rich the rules are, how fast revocation must be and where the content lives. Watch the winner change and read why.

most.why: Nearly every hit survives, so the top k stays full.

few.why: Hidden hits eat the top k, so you must over-fetch.

tiny.why: Most queries return one result or none unless you fetch thousands.

tag.why: Works, though a filter is cheaper.

group.why: Needs resolved groups in your code and an ACL lookup per hit.

rich.why: Code can evaluate any rule: deny, links, guests.

hours.why: Fine, but not the reason to choose it.

minutes.why: Can read a live ACL cache at check time.

seconds.why: Can consult a live source, but denied text has already reached your code.

most.why: Works, though the filter adds little when almost everything is visible.

few.why: Only allowed documents compete, so the top k stays full.

tiny.why: Recall under a very selective filter can degrade. Measure it.

tag.why: One filterable field does the job.

group.why: Group ids in a filter, resolved from the token or Graph.

rich.why: Allow-lists only. Deny entries and links must be flattened before indexing.

minutes.why: Bounded by your sync path. A pull indexer cannot beat 5 minutes.

seconds.why: An index copy lags the source.

copied.why: The ACL fields sit beside the chunks they guard.

system.why: Copying the content creates a sync problem you could avoid.

most.why: Live checks add latency for little gain.

few.why: Filter first, then verify the few survivors.

tiny.why: Few survivors keep the live check cheap.

tag.why: A tenant id needs no live check.

group.why: Catches membership changes the index has not seen.

rich.why: The source evaluates deny rules, links and guests exactly.

hours.why: Pays latency for freshness nobody asked for.

minutes.why: Closes most of the lag window.

seconds.why: The source of truth answers for every returned hit.

copied.why: Verifies the copy against its origin.

system.why: Reasonable, but delegation may be simpler.

few.why: The source ranks only what the caller can see.

tiny.why: Same, with no filtered ANN to tune.

rich.why: The source applies its own full rules.

seconds.why: Permissions are read at query time.

copied.why: Nothing to delegate to once the content is copied elsewhere.

system.why: The system of record answers with the caller's token.

few.why: Isolation makes selectivity a non-issue inside a tenant.

tiny.why: A per-user slice is perfectly selective, at a high price.

tag.why: A tenant id maps to one index.

group.why: Group access inside a tenant still needs a filter.

rich.why: Walls cannot express deny rules or links.

seconds.why: Cutting a tenant off is an access change with no per-document sync.

copied.why: The content is already copied, so splitting it is a layout choice.

system.why: Duplicates content per tenant instead of querying the source.

blocks.takeaway: Post-filtering wins only when almost everything is visible. Pre-filtering is the default for copied content with group ACLs. Add a live check for seconds-level revocation, delegate when the source can retrieve, and build walls only when the permission model is a tenant id.

items.symptom: Users with narrow access get two or three results when ten were expected.
items.cause: A post-filter over a selective permission model: eight of ten hits were removed after retrieval.
items.fix: Move the predicate into the query, or over-fetch with a cap (k_needed divided by the visible fraction) and alert on result count per query.

items.symptom: A revoked user still sees a document for hours.
items.cause: The ACL in the index lags the source, and no live check or cache TTL covers the gap.
items.fix: Set a revocation SLA per tier, push ACL merges on change events, live-check the top hits for restricted content and test with a revoked canary user.

items.symptom: Filtered vector queries return few or poor results although matching documents exist.
items.cause: ANN recall degrades under a highly selective filter.
items.fix: Measure recall at production selectivity against a brute-force baseline, raise candidate counts and consider exhaustive search for small partitions.

items.symptom: A result comes back unfiltered on one path only.
items.cause: The filter is missing from one code path, such as an agent tool call, or the index has no permission metadata so the header does nothing.
items.fix: Put one API gatekeeper in front of every store, apply the filter on every retrieval including those inside agent loops and add a canary test per path.

items.symptom: Denied text shows up in a rerank request or a log although the final answer was clean.
items.cause: Post-filtering lets denied text reach later stages before it is dropped.
items.fix: Filter before reranking and logging, or log identifiers only.

How it isolates
Wins when

rows: Service per tenant
A separate search service
Few large or regulated tenants, hardest separation
Cost and operations per tenant, poor fit for many small tenants [[r22]]
Index per tenant
A separate index in one service
Hundreds of tenants. S3 HD allows 1,000 indexes per partition and 3,000 per service [[r20]]
Per-tier caps: Basic 15, S1 50, S2 and S3 200
Shared index with a tenant filter
A mandatory tenant field on every chunk and query
Thousands of small tenants
One missed filter leaks across tenants, so it needs the API gatekeeper
Namespace per tenant (Pinecone)
Every read and write targets one namespace, and offboarding deletes it
Many tenants on a vector store with namespaces, 100 (Starter) to 1,000,000 (Enterprise) per serverless index
Vendor specific, and the query-cost argument is the vendor's own claim [[r34]]
Partition key per tenant (Cosmos DB)
Tenant id as the partition key. Hierarchical keys lift the 20 GB logical partition limit
Documents already in Cosmos DB
A partition key is a data layout choice, not an authorization control [[r33]]
Row-level security (Azure SQL, PostgreSQL)
A database predicate on every query, with the user passed through SESSION_CONTEXT
Content in a relational store and the app sets the user per request
Owners and BYPASSRLS roles bypass unless forced, and a shared login hides the user [[r31]] [[r32]]
blocks.caption: Azure's mixed model is documented: big tenants on dedicated services, small tenants on shared indexes [[r21]].

items.title: Go deeper: the security filter pattern and its limits

blocks.title: Security filter on a Collection(Edm.String) field
blocks.caption: The field is filterable and retrievable: false.

blocks.md: `search.in` equals a chain of `eq ... or` but is faster. The docs describe sub-second responses with hundreds or thousands of values and no explicit item cap, limited by request size (16 MB payload, 8 KB URL for GET), and latency grows with the value count [[r14]]. The pattern is a string match with no authentication, so your code must derive the principal from a validated token. `retrievable: false` hides the field from results but is not field-level security [[r13]].

blocks.title: What interviewers listen for
blocks.md: For each option, say which stage sees denied text and what flips the choice. A strong answer ends with the combination: pre-filter for the bulk, a live check for restricted tiers, a gatekeeper in front of every store and a canary test for every path.

quiz.q: Content sits in SharePoint with deny-style rules and sharing links, and revocation must take effect in seconds. Which option moves to the top?
options: Post-filter in your code against the indexed ACL copy of the permissions
Pre-filter in the index with flattened group ids from nightly syncs
Live-check the top hits at the source
An index per user rebuilt whenever a permission changes
quiz.explain: Only the source of truth evaluates deny rules and links exactly and is current within seconds. A post-filter over an indexed copy and a flattened pre-filter both inherit sync lag and cannot express deny entries. An index per user multiplies copies and still lags the source.

quiz.q: What is the most serious flaw in this handler?
options: The client supplies its own groups
`search.in` is slower than a chain of `eq` clauses for long lists
The ACL field should be marked retrievable so it can be filtered
The filter should run after the search instead of before it
quiz.explain: The principal comes from the request body, so the filter enforces whatever the client claims. Groups must be derived from a validated token or Graph, and quotes in values need escaping. `search.in` is the faster form, retrievable is not needed for filtering, and moving the filter after the search would make it a post-filter.

quiz.q: After launch the median user gets one result instead of ten. Telemetry for the median user is shown. What is the cause?
options: Embedding model drift after the last re-index
A reranker timeout under heavy load
A recall floor in the pre-filter
quiz.explain: Fetching 30 candidates at 5% visibility leaves about 1.5 visible documents, which matches 29 of 30 removed. The fix is a pre-filter, or an over-fetch near 10 divided by 0.05, which is 200. Drift and timeouts do not show up as ACL removals, and a pre-filter would not report removals at all.

quiz.q: A product serves 40 enterprise tenants. A few are 100 times larger than the rest, each contract requires deletion within days, and access inside a tenant is only membership of the tenant. Which wall fits?
options: Index per tenant, big ones on own services
Shared index with a mandatory tenant filter and delete-by-query offboarding
An index per user with tenants as folders
A post-filter in your code with tenant ids in metadata
quiz.explain: Forty tenants fit well inside per-tier index caps, dropping an index satisfies deletion, and skewed sizes match the documented mixed model of dedicated services for large tenants. A shared index makes deletion a delete-by-query and bets on one filter never being missed. An index per user has no tenant meaning, and a post-filter isolates nothing.

takeaways: Ask which stage sees denied text. Post-filters expose the most stages, pre-filters the fewest.
Post-filtering needs a visible fraction near 1. Over-fetch is k_needed divided by that fraction.
Pre-filter for copied content with group ACLs, add a live check for seconds-level revocation.
Delegate to the source when it can retrieve with the caller's token, and walls fit only tenant-id permission models.
One gatekeeper in front of every store, and a canary test per code path.
